paras: The lynching of Jim Carr took place in Hancock County, Mississippi, in late December 1903, when a mob took Carr, a Black man held for shooting Deputy Marshal Cobb at Saucier, from the officer who was moving him at night to the county jail at McHenry, and killed him. Accounts differed on whether he was hanged or shot to death, and on whether the shooting of Cobb happened on Christmas Day or the day after. The case ran as a short item in white newspapers from New York to Nevada and South Carolina, most of them carrying a New Orleans wire dispatch that called Carr "Cobb's slayer."

Saucier was described as a station on the G. & S. I. Railroad and as a small town five miles south of McHenry, where the county jail was said to be "safe against attacks." According to a McHenry dispatch to the New-York Tribune, Carr went hunting on Christmas Day and came back to his home in Saucier "very drunk and boisterous." Deputy Marshal Walker Cobb ordered him to keep quiet "under pain of arrest."

In the Tribune's account, Carr "shot at" Cobb, and the marshal fired back, wounding him, and placed him under arrest. A New Orleans dispatch gave a fuller version, saying Carr had been disturbing the peace and shot Cobb when the officer tried to arrest him, "killing him instantly," after which the marshal of Saucier wounded Carr and locked him in the town jail.

A mob gathered, but the marshal prevented a first attempt to lynch the prisoner. Fearing that the mob would return, he kept Carr hidden until night and then set out with him for the county jail at McHenry. On the way the mob waylaid them in the pine woods and took the prisoner from the marshal. The New Orleans dispatch said Carr was hanged at Millview, while the Tribune and two Mississippi papers said the mob shot him to death.

None of the reports named any member of the mob, and no report of arrests, an inquest or a grand jury inquiry was found. The Greene County Herald at Leakesville carried only word of "the shooting of Walter Cobb, a wellknown citizen," at Saucier, without mention of Carr or the mob.

The New-York Tribune printed the first report on December 27 under the headline "MISSISSIPPI MOB SHOOTS NEGRO" and the deck "He Got Drunk on a Christmas Hunt and Shot at Marshal." The next day the New Orleans dispatch appeared in the San Francisco Call as "MOB LYNCHES COBB'S SLAYER," with a deck saying the marshal had failed "to Save Life of a Negro Murderer," and in the New York Sun as "MOB LYNCHES A NEGRO." The same story was reprinted as "Negro Murderer Lynched" in the Daily Silver State of Winnemucca, Nevada, on December 29, and in the Penn's Grove Record of New Jersey and the Abbeville Press and Banner of South Carolina in January.

These versions gave the killing of Cobb as fact and told the story from the marshal's side, with no word from or about Carr beyond the charge. In Mississippi, the Brandon News gave the lynching a single line in a roundup of wire news, and the Brookhaven Leader, in a column of state items, called Carr "the murderer" but ended by describing him as "a hard working and highly respected young man." The case appeared only in white papers, from the Tribune's first report to the Abbeville reprint more than two weeks later; no Black newspaper account of it was found.

The New Orleans dispatch, dated December 27, said Cobb was killed "yesterday" and Carr lynched "last night," placing both on December 26. The McHenry telegraph, filed a day earlier, put the hunt and the shooting on Christmas Day, as did the Brookhaven Leader.

On the manner of death, the New Orleans dispatch said Carr was hanged, while the McHenry telegraph, the report filed nearest the scene, and both Mississippi papers said he was shot. The Tribune said only that Carr "shot at" Cobb and did not report his death, and the Greene County Herald named the wounded man as Walter Cobb, a citizen rather than an officer.

reader.title: Lynching of Jim Carr
bases: A mob took Carr, a prisoner accused of shooting a deputy marshal, from the officer moving him to the county jail and killed him (A1, A2, A3, A6).

Every report says a 'mob' seized Carr from an officer and hanged or shot him without legal process (A1, A2, A3, A5, A6); the papers present the killing as retribution for his alleged killing of Deputy Marshal Cobb (A2, A3).

A McHenry telegraph to the New-York Tribune (A1), a separate New Orleans dispatch (A2, A3) and a Brookhaven, Miss., state-news brief (A5) agree that a mob took Carr from the officer and killed him, though they differ on method and date.

accounts.gist: Carr came home drunk from a Christmas hunt, shot at Deputy Marshal Walker Cobb when ordered to keep quiet, was wounded and arrested; the marshal hid him until night, and a mob intercepted them on the way to McHenry and shot him to death.

accounts.label: New Orleans wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Carr, disturbing the peace, shot and instantly killed Cobb when arrested; the marshal stopped a first lynching attempt, but a mob waylaid him in the pine woods on the way to McHenry and hanged Carr at Millview.

accounts.label: Mississippi state-news briefs
accounts.gist: Carr killed Cobb (on Christmas day, per the Brookhaven Leader) at Saucier and was taken from an officer by a mob and shot to death; the Leader added that he was 'hard working and highly respected'.

accounts.label: Greene County Herald
accounts.gist: Reports only that Walter Cobb, 'a wellknown citizen', was shot at Saucier.

framing.detail: The New Orleans dispatch ran under 'MOB LYNCHES COBB'S SLAYER' with the deck 'Marshal of Mississippi Town Fails in Attempt to Save Life of a Negro Murderer', and as 'MOB LYNCHES A NEGRO.', treating Carr's guilt as settled.
The Tribune headed its McHenry telegraph 'MISSISSIPPI MOB SHOOTS NEGRO.' and 'He Got Drunk on a Christmas Hunt and Shot at Marshal.'
The Brookhaven Leader called Carr 'the murderer' yet closed its brief by calling him 'a hard working and highly respected young man.'
The Brandon News gave the lynching one line in a wire roundup between foreign and national items.

conflicts.note: The shooting version comes from the McHenry-datelined Tribune telegraph, the report filed nearest the scene, and both Mississippi papers; the hanging version is the New Orleans dispatch.
